profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the Developer Productivity group and the Checkout team to prepare a six-week pilot that moves Checkout from a GitFlow-style release process toward a more trunk-based workflow. Context: the company wants evidence from a real product team before standardizing Git guidance across engineering, and Checkout was chosen because it has frequent changes but a manageable team size. Agenda: align on which repositories are included in the pilot, how existing release work will coexist with the new flow, what "green on main" means operationally, and how approval rules will be carried over into the new setup. Expected outcome: both participants leave believing they have agreed on the pilot scope, branch handoff, protection settings, and readiness criteria for the cutover.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: CI/CD platforms, GitHub governance, repository templates, developer workflow rollout
members.background: Priya leads internal tooling changes across product teams and recently built the company's standard GitHub rulesets for protected branches and required checks.
members.private_state: She wants the Checkout pilot to be low-friction and comparable to other pilots, so she is trying to keep it narrowly scoped to one repository and reuse existing org-level templates without making team-specific exceptions.
hidden_assumptions: "Green on main" means all required GitHub checks on the merge commit pass, plus the standard smoke test after deploy.
When a product team says "the checkout repo," they usually mean the primary application repository unless companion repos are explicitly called out.
In conversations about migration, "the release branch" refers to the centrally scheduled release-train branch created by Release Engineering.
"Same approval rule as today" can be implemented by carrying over the intent through the org ruleset on main, even if the exact branch path changes.
A trunk-based pilot should not include extra repos or bespoke approval flows unless someone flags them directly.

members.name: Lucas Almeida
members.expertise: Service delivery, release coordination, payment systems, cross-repo team operations
members.background: Lucas manages the backend engineers responsible for checkout flows and has been running a branch-based process with a dedicated integration path for quarterly commercial initiatives.
members.private_state: He wants the team to appear supportive of the pilot while avoiding any disruption to an important renewals release already underway, and he wants to preserve the risk controls his senior engineers rely on.
hidden_assumptions: "Green on main" means the code is effectively release-safe for Checkout, including the nightly end-to-end purchase journey and operational confidence for on-call.
The team's delivery unit includes the application repo, the shared API-contract repo, and the deployment chart repo, even if people casually use the singular "repo."
When people say "the release branch" in Checkout discussions, they mean the team's active long-lived branch for the enterprise renewals work.
"Same approval rule as today" means the same number of human sign-offs the team currently requires before changes move forward.
If a workflow change is described as applying to Checkout, the associated repos and branch habits will naturally be carried along unless someone excludes them.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the pilot is safe as long as "main stays green."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes "green" means the required GitHub Actions checks and the standard post-merge smoke test pass on the main branch.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes "green" means Checkout is truly release-safe, which in practice includes the nightly end-to-end purchase journey and confidence that on-call will not see latent breakage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: "Green" is a deeply familiar engineering term, and each participant assumes the other is using the ordinary team-wide meaning rather than a workflow-specific one.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in "the Checkout pilot"
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss setting up "the Checkout pilot" or "the pilot repo" as if it were one obvious unit.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the pilot covers only the primary repository, `checkout-service`, because that is the artifact governed by her standard migration template.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the pilot naturally includes `checkout-service`, `checkout-contracts`, and `checkout-deploy`, because his team ships them as one coordinated delivery unit.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Teams often refer to a service and its adjacent repos as a single thing in casual speech, so the singular phrasing sounds normal and does not invite clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that "the release branch" can stay open during the cutover.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the central release-train branch `release/2024.10`, which Release Engineering created for the monthly train.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the team's active branch `release/q4-renewals`, which contains customer-specific renewal work his team is stabilizing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each participant has a single highly salient release branch in mind, so the definite phrase "the release branch" feels precise enough even though they are referencing different branches.

misalignment_points.topic: How to preserve "the same approval rule"
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they will keep "the same approval rule as today" during the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to enforce one CODEOWNER approval plus required checks through the org-level GitHub ruleset on `main`, because that is the standard mechanism for trunk-style repos.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the team will continue its current practice of getting two human approvals before anything significant lands, regardless of how the branch model changes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They appear aligned on preserving rigor, and the phrase "same approval rule" masks that one is talking about GitHub enforcement mechanics while the other is thinking about the team's social review habit.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to look like the other trunk-based pilots: one repo, standard org-level ruleset, minimal exceptions. For Checkout, that means I can get checkout-service onto the migration template and avoid dragging in companion repos unless Lucas explicitly insists. If we align on the pilot repo, the release branch overlap, and what ready-for-cutover means, I can keep this narrow and low-friction.
